```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

This tutorial walks through the package on French female death rates, ages 0 to 100, years 1901 to 2006. Each section shows one function.

## 1. Data

Curves go in a matrix with grid points in rows and time in columns. Here the rows are ages and the columns are years.

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ffarfima)
library(demography)
```

```{r}
x <- log10(smooth.demogdata(extract.years(fr.mort, 1901:2006))$rate$female[1:101, ])
dim(x)
```

## 2. Split the curves: `split_curves()`

The training block is used to estimate the model, the validation block to calibrate the prediction bands, and the optional test block to score the forecasts. The blocks follow each other in time.

```{r}
blocks <- split_curves(x, train = 0.6, valid = 0.2)
sapply(blocks, ncol)
```

## 3. Fit the model: `ffarfima()`

`ffarfima()` does everything that is learned from data: it estimates `d`, selects `(p, q)`, fits the operators, and calibrates the prediction bands on the validation block for horizons 1 to `h`.

```{r}
fit <- ffarfima(blocks$train, blocks$valid,
                d = "bc_lpwn2", order = "ic_full", p = 0:5, q = 0:5,
                h = 10, level = c(0.8, 0.95), band = c("SR", "NS", "AC"),
                trim = 20, seed = 1)
fit
```

The estimated model:

```{r}
fit$d
fit$order
```

The fit object holds the model, the in-sample fit and the details of each step:

```{r}
names(fit)
```

`fitted(fit)` is the in-sample one-step-ahead fit on the scale of the data, and `fitted(fit, scale = "differenced")` the fit of the short-memory part on the fractionally differenced scale. Both are uncentred. The residuals are the same on both scales, and `fitted(fit) + residuals(fit)` gives the training curves.

```{r}
round(fitted(fit)[1:3, 1:4], 3)
round(fitted(fit, scale = "differenced")[1:3, 1:4], 4)
round(residuals(fit)[1:3, 1:4], 4)
```

All choices are made in this one call:

| Argument | What it sets | Options |
|---|---|---|
| `d` | memory estimator, or a known value | `"bc_lpwn2"`, `"bc_lpwn1"`, `"lpwn2"`, `"lpwn1"`, `"lw"`, `"dfa"`, or a number |
| `order` | order selection, or known orders | `"ic_full"`, `"ic_auto"`, `"bj"`, `"cv"`, or `c(p, q)` |
| `p`, `q` | the orders searched | e.g. `0:5` |
| `method` | operator estimator | `"farma"`, or `"far"` for the FAR(1) benchmark |
| `h` | longest forecast horizon | the validation block needs at least `h + 1` curves |
| `level` | coverage levels of the bands | e.g. `c(0.8, 0.95)` |
| `band` | which prediction bands | `"SR"` scaled residual, `"NS"` split conformal, `"AC"` adaptive conformal |
| `window` | estimation window at each forecast origin | `"expanding"` or `"fixed"` |
| `trim` | differenced curves dropped before estimation | about 15 to 30 for 50 to 100 training curves |
| `memory_args`, `order_args` | settings passed to `estimate_memory()` and `select_order()` | e.g. `list(B = 50)`, `list(n_lags = 10)` |

### Choosing the conformal method

The bands are chosen in `ffarfima()` with `band`. To use only the adaptive conformal band:

```{r}
fit_ac <- ffarfima(blocks$train, blocks$valid, band = "AC", trim = 20, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
fit_ac
```

### Other estimators, known values and the benchmark

```{r}
fit_lw <- ffarfima(blocks$train, blocks$valid, d = "lw", order = "bj", trim = 20, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
fit_lw$d
fit_lw$order

fit_known <- ffarfima(blocks$train, blocks$valid, d = 1, order = c(1, 0), trim = 20, verbose = FALSE)
fit_known$order

bench <- ffarfima(blocks$train, blocks$valid, d = 1, method = "far", trim = 20, verbose = FALSE)
bench
```

### Without a validation block

With `valid = NULL` the model is still estimated, but no bands can be calibrated, so only point forecasts are possible. Cross-validation is not available either, because it needs validation curves.

```{r}
fit_point <- ffarfima(blocks$train, d = "lw", trim = 20, verbose = FALSE)
fit_point
```

```{r, error = TRUE}
ffarfima(blocks$train, order = "cv", trim = 20, verbose = FALSE)
```

## 4. Forecast and evaluate: `predict()`

`predict()` applies the fitted model. Without `test`, it forecasts `h` steps after the last curve the fit has seen, which is the end of the validation block (1984).

```{r}
fc_future <- predict(fit)
fc_future
```

With `test`, it forecasts from every test year using all earlier curves, compares the forecasts with what was observed, and then forecasts beyond the test block.

```{r}
fc <- predict(fit, test = blocks$test)
fc
```

The results are stored in the forecast object:

```{r}
names(fc)
names(fc$evaluation)
round(fc$point_forecast[1:3, 1:4], 3)
round(fc$bands$AC[["95%"]]$upper[1:3, 1:4], 3)
fc$evaluation$point
head(fc$evaluation$interval)
head(fc$evaluation$wis)
```

`h` can be smaller than in the fit, and `band` can keep a subset of the fit's bands:

```{r}
fc_ac5 <- predict(fit, test = blocks$test, h = 5, band = "AC", verbose = FALSE)
fc_ac5$evaluation$interval
```

A fit without a validation block gives point forecasts and point accuracy only. Its test block must follow the training curves, so here it is the validation and test years together:

```{r}
fc_point <- predict(fit_point, test = cbind(blocks$valid, blocks$test), h = 5)
fc_point
```

If a block does not follow the previous one in time, the package warns:

```{r}
fc_wrong <- predict(fit_point, test = blocks$test, h = 5, verbose = FALSE)
```

## 5. Plot: `plot()`

Without `target_test_curve`, `plot()` draws the forecast beyond the data. With `target_test_curve = k`, it draws the forecast of the k-th test curve that was made `h` steps earlier, against the observed curve. Here that is the forecast of 1995 made from 1992.

```{r, fig.height = 4}
plot(fc, h = 1, band = "AC", xlab = "Age", ylab = "log10 death rate")
```

```{r, fig.height = 4}
plot(fc, h = 3, target_test_curve = 11, band = "AC", level = 0.95, xlab = "Age", ylab = "log10 death rate")
```

## 6. Tables: `as.data.frame()`

```{r}
head(as.data.frame(fc), 3)
df_test <- as.data.frame(fc, test = TRUE)
head(df_test, 3)
```

The share of observed points inside the 95% AC band at `h = 1`, which matches the ECP above:

```{r}
ac95 <- subset(df_test, band == "AC" & level == 0.95 & h == 1)
mean(ac95$observed >= ac95$lower & ac95$observed <= ac95$upper)
```

## 7. Estimate `d` on its own: `estimate_memory()`

```{r}
m <- estimate_memory(blocks$train, method = "bc_lpwn2", seed = 1)
m
sapply(c("dfa", "lw", "lpwn1", "lpwn2"), function(meth) estimate_memory(blocks$train, method = meth)$d)
```

The notes say that LPWN stopped at the edge of its search range (0.01 to 0.99 for each round of differencing), so here `d` is only known to be close to one.

## 8. Select the orders on their own: `select_order()`

```{r}
select_order(blocks$train, d = m, method = "ic_full", trim = 20)
select_order(blocks$train, d = m, method = "bj", trim = 20, seed = 1)
select_order(blocks$train, d = m, method = "cv", valid = blocks$valid, h = 5, trim = 20)
```

`"ic_auto"` takes its noise level from the largest candidate. When that model is unstable it warns, and a smaller range works:

```{r}
o_auto <- select_order(blocks$train, d = m, method = "ic_auto", trim = 20)
select_order(blocks$train, d = m, method = "ic_auto", p = 0:3, q = 0:3, trim = 20)
```

## 9. Simulated data: `sim_ffarfima()`

Curves from a known FARFIMA(1, 0.3, 0) model. They have no column names, which works the same way.

```{r}
sim <- sim_ffarfima(n = 500, d = 0.3, p = 1, q = 0, ar_strength = 0.5, seed = 1)
sb <- split_curves(sim$X)
fit_sim <- ffarfima(sb$train, sb$valid, d = "lpwn2", h = 5, trim = 50, verbose = FALSE)
fit_sim$d
fit_sim$order
```

## 10. Fractional differencing: `frac_diff()`

A negative `d` integrates, so applying `-d` afterwards gives back the original curves.

```{r}
y <- frac_diff(blocks$train, d = 1.086)
max(abs(frac_diff(y, d = -1.086) - blocks$train))
```
